title: The Eternal Sonship Distinct from Creation
english: Or again, in the distinction the Son bears toward creation, he declares: the Son is indeed the Son, but the created things are slaves. The Son, as Son, sits at the Father’s right hand; but the created things, as slaves, stand ready, are dispatched, and render service.

Given that these things are written in this way, the Son is not to be understood as begotten from them, O Arians; on the contrary, he is truly another—indeed, one of the created order in origin, yet properly belonging to the Father, dwelling in the Father’s bosom.

Moreover, the very wording here—‘Having become’—does not intend to mark the Son as unbegotten, as you mistakenly suppose. For if he had merely said ‘Having become’ and then fallen silent, that might have given you a pretext.

But since he had already affirmed the title ‘Son’ and demonstrated throughout this passage that the Son is essentially distinct from the created things, he did not leave the term ‘Having become’ isolated or insignificant; rather, he bound it to the greater reality.

For he regarded the word as indifferent in weight. Knowing full well that when one speaks of ‘Having become’ in reference to a genuine Son, the meaning is equivalent to ‘having been begotten’—and thus affirms the Son’s superiority—he declares it accordingly.
For the created thing, in its very nature, does not differ whether one says it ‘has come to be’ or ‘has been made.’

But the created things, as they are mere creations, cannot properly be called begotten—unless, that is, they have somehow received a share in the begotten Son, and thus, by participation, are spoken of as begotten themselves.
And this, too, the divine Scripture acknowledges: when speaking of the created things, it declares, ‘All things came to be through him,’ and ‘All things were made in wisdom.’

Indeed, when we look at sons born according to nature—like Job’s seven sons and three daughters, or Abraham, who was a hundred years old when Isaac was born to him—we see a clear distinction. Those born in the course of nature are one kind of thing, but the substance of the Father alone is the proper offspring of the Son. Therefore, the Arians’ pretext concerning the one who became is refuted. Even if, ashamed of this, they try again to speak comparatively, claiming that the things said are spoken only in comparison and that therefore the things compared must be of the same kind, they would still be ashamed beforehand, just like those who follow Valentinus and Carpocrates. For one of them says the angels are consubstantial with Christ, while the other says the angels of the world are creators. And perhaps these Arians, having learned from them, now compare the Word of God to the angels. Yet they would be ashamed to imagine such things, especially when the hymn-singer asks, 'Who shall be likened to the Lord among the sons of God?' and 'Who is like you among the gods, O Lord?' Still, if they were to learn, they would find that among consubstantial beings, likeness is commonly affirmed in comparison, but not among those of different kinds. For no one would compare God to man, or man to the irrational beasts, or wood to stone, because of the utter dissimilarity of their natures. Rather, God is an incomparable thing in Himself, while man is compared to man, wood to wood, and stone to stone. And concerning these things, no one would say 'the stronger,' but only 'the more' or 'the greater.' Thus Joseph was more handsome than his brothers, and Rachel than Leah; and one star is not stronger than another.

Therefore, the Son’s relation to the Father cannot be understood by comparing Him to creatures, even the highest, for such comparison assumes a likeness of nature that does not exist. The Arians err by treating the eternal Son as if He were merely the greatest among creatures, like the most handsome man.

title: Nature of the Son
english: but rather "differs in glory" (1 Corinthians 15:41). With things of different kinds, however, when someone sets them side by side, then "better" is said of what is different, as it is said of wisdom and of stones (Proverbs 8:11). So if the apostle had said, "By so much more the Son goes before the angels," or "by so much is he greater," you would have had a pretext, on the ground that the Son was being compared with the angels. But as it is, by saying that he is better, and differs by as much as a son stands apart from servants, he shows that he is other than the nature of the angels. And again, by saying that he is the one who laid the foundation of all things (Hebrews 1:10), he shows that he is other than all the things that have come into being. And since he is other than the nature of things that have come into being, and of a different substance, what comparison or likeness can his substance have with the things that have come into being? This is why the Son himself did not say, "My Father is better than I," so that no one would take him to be a stranger to the Father's nature. He said "greater" (John 14:28), not by any size or by time, but because of his begetting from the Father himself. And yet in saying "is greater" he showed once more that the substance is his own.

The apostle too, when he said, "having become so much better than the angels" (Hebrews 1:4), did not mean first of all to set the substance of the Word apart from the things that have come into being; for it admits no comparison, or rather it is something other. He was looking to the Word's economy in the flesh, and to the economy he carried out at that time, and wanted to show that he is not like those who came before. So, by as much as he differs in nature from those he had sent before, by so much more the grace that came from him and through him would be better than the ministry carried out through angels. For it was the part of servants only to demand the fruits, but of the Son and Master to forgive the debts and to hand the vineyard over to others.

These things, then, are enough to shame those who fight against the truth. But perhaps, because it is written "having become better," they will not hear "having become," said of the Son, as equal to "is," nor take "having become" to refer to the better ministry that came about and understand it as we have said; perhaps they think that this word says the Word is a thing that came into being. Then let them hear again. If the Son is one of the angels, let "having become" be said of him as of them, and let him differ from them in nothing by nature. Then either they too are sons, or he too is an angel; and either let them all sit together at the right hand of the Father, or let the Son too stand with all of them as a ministering spirit, himself sent on ministries like theirs. But if Paul sets the Son apart from the things that have come into being, saying, "For to which of the angels did he ever say, 'You are my Son, today I have begotten you'? And again, 'I will be to him a father, and he shall be to me a son'" (Hebrews 1:5) […]

"And when he again brings in the firstborn" (Hebrews 1:6). title: The Co-eternity of the Son
english: …That is, from the earth; a staining of garments from Bosporus?"—a term which in the Greek tongue signifies compression or affliction—"that your garments and your clothing are red, as if from the tread of a winepress?" They were approaching him there, saying, "What are these wounds which are in the midst of your hands?" And he replied to them, "As I was struck in my beloved house." No one would have clearly asserted that it was necessary for him to retain the marks of the nails after the resurrection and to ascend into heaven with them.
It is more worthy to contemplate that matter.

Just as he showed the side to the unbelieving Thomas, along with the marks of the nails, so that he might finally believe and say with a learning mind, "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28), so also he appeared through the signs of the passion, making the manner of the economy after the flesh manifest to the holy angels. Indeed, he bore red garments and the marks of the nails so that they too might believe that, being by nature and truly existing God, he had become a son of man, having taken a body from the holy Virgin and having seated himself in self-emptying, so that, having offered himself as a sacrifice and a victim for all as a fragrance of sweetness to God and the Father, he might save those under heaven.

The holy multitude of the angels also worships him. They do not refuse this worship because he was a firstborn and a man among many brothers, but having been taught the economy, they recognize the Son from God according to nature and the moment when he became flesh.
…But to the Son: "Your throne, O God" (Psalm 45:6).

How, then, is it not foolish and impudent to scrutinize that nature through which all things were provided toward existence, a nature older than all time? For through it the Word has come to be, and before all ages, the Word is from God the Father.
Yet the wanderers accuse him of being recent, claiming that he is a created being, not realizing that they are opposing the words of the Holy Spirit.
For those who speak in the Spirit say that the ages were made through him.
But those who insist he is a created being base their argument on what lies beyond intellect and reason, failing to grasp even that through the lens of intellect.
For God did not become Father within time, but he was always so, even in the beginning.
Since this is the case, it is a necessity in every respect to conceive of the Son as co-existing, so that God may truly be called Father.

Since they have taught that if the Son is the Word of the Father, and wisdom, and power, and the character and radiance of his subsistence, then what sort of time was it during which the Father was without the Logos, lacking the Son? When was the source of wisdom without wisdom itself? When was power without its power? When was the radiance of his glory not present in God? Or how could his own character not be continuously with him and in him? If indeed these things came to pass within time, then he was not Father before he was begotten; he would have been without Logos, without wisdom, and without strength, lacking both character and radiance.
But I consider it impious to conceive of such a thing, and it is the highest impiety…
